newsitem.title: USA: Oscars day minus one - Hollywood gets ready.
newsitem.headline: Oscars day minus one - Hollywood gets ready.

text.p: The stage was being readied on Sunday, workers were laying the red carpet and fans were camped out ready for Hollywood's big night out -- the Academy Awards.

But as hairdressers and tuxedo rental stores were doing brisk business, Monday's Oscars show was embroiled in controversy. The focus was not on who would be at the ceremony, but, rather, who would not.
In an apparent snub to the Acacdemy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Barbra Streisand will not sing the Oscar-nominated song from "The Mirror Has Two Faces."
A spokeswoman for the academy told Reuters that Streisand pulled out and was not expected to attend. Natalie Cole will sing "I Finally Found Someone" instead.
Some news reports said Streisand was upset that the film, which she directed and co-produced, was passed over for a best picture nod.

Another no-show will be Hustler magazine publisher Larry Flynt, whose life was portrayed in the movie "The People v Larry Flynt." He claimed Sony, the parent company of Columbia Pictures, had no ticket for him to attend.

However, Flynt, who has been attacked as a pornographer by feminist groups, was at the Golden Globes award ceremony in January with actor Woody Harrelson, who played him in the film, and Courtney Love, who played his late wife Althea.
But for the Academy Awards, where Harrelson has been nominated for best actor and Milos Forman for best director, Columbia said it had no ticket for Flynt.
"The ironic thing about all this is that this film is about censorship," Flynt told the Los Angeles Times.
Unfazed, the first 1,000 fans in line -- some had been waiting since Wednesday -- were admitted on Saturday to bleachers set up at the arrivals area outside the Shrine Auditorium.

That meant they would spend two nights camped on wooden benches with blankets, flasks, coolers and cameras. There they will watch on Monday as their favourite stars step out of limousines and stroll the red carpet.
In a year with few big-name stars nominated, competition appeared wide open. The only Oscar certainty seemed to be Lauren Bacall as best supporting actress for "The Mirror Has Two Faces."

Much like Paul Newman's win as best actor in 1986 for "The Colour of Money," Bacall was a sentimental favourite for an Oscar as a reward for 50 years in Hollywood without a nomination, despite indelible appearances opposite Humphrey Bogart.

The buzz in Hollywood this year? According to the Los Angeles Times, there is no buzz. "Maybe it's because the people up for awards don't have a lot of enemies or friends in this town," one producer told the newspaper.
Indeed, in the major categories, only Tom Cruise -- best actor nominee for "Jerry Maguire" -- and Dianne Keaton -- best actress nominee for "Marvin's Room" -- are A-list stars.
Harrelson, Ralph Fiennes (best actor for "The English Patient") and James Woods (best supporting actor for "Ghosts of Mississippi") are B-list performers, but the rest?

The average movie fan would be hard-pressed to identify Brenda Blethyn ("Secrets & Lies"), Frances McDormand ("Fargo"), Kristin Scott Thomas ("The English Patient") or Emily Watson ("Breaking the Waves") as best actress.
For best actor, neither Billy Bob Thornton ("Sling Blade") nor Geoffrey Rush ("Shine") are household names.
The supporting actor category is completed by first-time nominees, Cuba Gooding Jr. ("Jerry Maguire"), William Macy ("Fargo"), Armin Mueller-Stahl ("Shine") and Edward Norton ("Primal Fear").

Besides Bacall, the supporting actress group has Joan Allen ("The Crucible"), who was nominated last year for "Nixon," and Barbara Hershey ("The Portrait of a Lady"), who is certainly a recognisable actress.
But Juliette Binoche ("The English Patient") and Marianne Jean-Baptiste ("Secrets & Lies") are unknowns.

If precedents mean anything, then "The English Patient", which picked up 12 nominations, had a good chance of winning best picture. In the last 25 years, the film with the most nominations won the best picture Oscar 21 times.
Director Anthony Minghella said the film "treats audiences as grownups -- it asks them to think and feel."

The 12 nominations, he said at a nominees' luncheon last week, were like 12 arrows pointing movie-goers in the direction of the film. "And that means we have more chance of a dialogue in the dark with the audience," Minghella said.
